Both gain speed at the same rate.

flow.context: In this step, you drop a full bottle and an empty bottle together.

flow.do: Ask your child to say why heavy and light things fell together. Then read the note for the parent.
flow.say: Say it in your own words. Why did the full bottle and the empty bottle land together?
flow.kid: Say why the two bottles landed together.
flow.parent: After your child has answered: the Earth pulls the full bottle harder, but the full bottle has more mass, so it needs a bigger force to speed up in the same way. The bigger pull and the bigger mass cancel, so both gain speed at the same rate. This is the second law at work. Without air, a feather and a hammer would fall together too.
flow.context: In this step, you explain why heavy and light things fall together.

activities.title: Soft Hands: why do we pull our hands back to catch?
activities.context: In this activity, you catch a soft ball with stiff hands and then with hands that move back. Then you try a tiny jump with straight legs and with bent knees. You feel how a longer stop gives a smaller force.

materials.item: a soft ball, such as a tennis ball or a ball of rolled socks
a helper to toss the ball gently from 2 metres away
a bottom stair or a low step about 15 centimetres high, and a non-slip floor

schedule.what: Catch with stiff hands, then with hands that move back. Jump down one low step with straight legs, then with bent knees. Say which felt softer.

activities.safety: Use a soft ball, never a cricket ball. The jump is a tiny step-down only, with a grown-up beside you, on a non-slip floor. Stop if your knees hurt.
activities.record: Give each catch a score from 1 (soft) to 5 (sharp) and do 3 catches of each kind. Draw a pair of pictures for the catch and a pair for the jump. Under each, write 'soft' or 'sharp' for how it felt.

setup.art: A boy catching a soft ball with stiff hands held out in front of him, not moving.
setup.caption: 1. Catch the ball with stiff hands that do not move.

setup.art: The same boy catching the ball with his hands drawn back towards his chest as it arrives.
setup.caption: 2. Catch again, and pull your hands back as the ball arrives.

setup.art: A girl stepping down one low stair with straight legs, and then with bent knees, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 3. Step down from a low stair with straight legs, then with bent knees.

flow.do: Show the ball. Ask your child which will feel gentler: a catch with stiff hands or a catch with hands that move back. Ask why.
flow.say: A fielder pulls her hands back when she catches a fast ball. Which catch do you think feels gentler, stiff hands or hands that move back? Why?
flow.kid: Which catch is gentler, stiff hands or hands that move back? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think the fielder pulls her hands back?
good: So the ball does not hurt.
So the catch is softer.
So the ball stops more slowly.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soft Hands. You guess before you catch.

flow.do: The helper tosses the ball gently from 2 metres. Catch it 3 times with stiff hands that do not move. Then catch it 3 times, pulling your hands back as it arrives. Feel the difference.
flow.say: First, catch it with stiff hands. Feel the ball hit. Now catch it again, but pull your hands back as it arrives. Which felt softer?
flow.kid: Catch the ball with stiff hands. Then catch it and pull your hands back. Which feels softer?
flow.parent: Use an underarm toss, not hard. The pulled-back catch should feel gentler, though a soft ball may not sting either way. If you feel no difference, move the ball a little faster. Let the catcher give each catch a score from 1 (soft) to 5 (sharp), and compare the averages. With 2 to 4 children: one tosses, one catches, one writes the scores. Swap after each set.

check.q: Why does pulling your hands back make the catch feel softer?
options: The ball takes longer to stop, so the force on your hands is smaller
The ball becomes lighter
The ball is slower before it arrives
check.why: The ball goes from its speed to zero either way. When your hands move back, the stop takes more time. A change in motion spread over more time needs a smaller force. The ball did not get lighter or slower.

flow.context: In this step, you catch the ball two ways and feel the difference.

flow.do: A grown-up stands beside you. Step down off the low stair with straight legs, and feel the landing. Then step down with your knees bent, and feel the landing. Do each twice.
flow.say: Step down off the stair, once with straight legs and once with bent knees. Which landing is gentler? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Step down once with straight legs. Step down once with bent knees. Which is gentler?
flow.parent: Make it a tiny step, about 15 centimetres. Never jump from a height. The bent knee landing should feel softer in the legs and the head. Stop if your child complains of pain. Only one child steps at a time; the others watch and say which landing looked and sounded softer.
flow.context: In this step, you step down from a low stair in two ways, and feel the landing.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first. Then read the note for the parent.
flow.say: Your body has to stop in both cases. What did your hands and your knees do to make it gentler?
flow.kid: Your hands and knees made the stop longer. Why does that help?

ask.q: What do the fielder's hands and your bent knees have in common?
good: They make the stop take longer.
They give a bit as the force arrives.
They spread the stop over more time.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: stopping the same motion over a longer time needs a smaller force. This is why helmets have foam, cars have crumple zones, and a trampoline is kinder than a concrete floor.
flow.context: In this step, you find what the catch and the jump have in common.

activities.title: The Lift Scale: do you weigh more when the lift starts?
activities.context: In this activity, you stand on a bathroom scale in a lift and watch the number as the lift starts and stops. You use it if your building has a lift. A grown-up must come with you.

materials.item: a bathroom scale, a dial one if you have it (no lift in your building? You can still do the knee-bend version below)
a lift in your building, used at a quiet time
a grown-up, and a phone to film the scale if you have one
a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Weigh yourself at home. Ride the lift up and down while standing on the scale. Write the highest and lowest numbers. Say why the number changed.

activities.safety: A grown-up must come. Use the lift at a quiet time, hold the rail, stand still and do not jump. Do not hold the lift door open. Put the scale flat on the floor away from the door gap, and step on and off it slowly. At home, do the knee-bend near a wall or a grown-up so you cannot fall off the scale.
activities.record: Write the number at rest, the highest number and the lowest number going up, and the same going down. Draw a small picture of the lift with an arrow for the direction.

setup.art: A girl standing on a bathroom scale in a flat, with a pencil and paper beside it, reading the number.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh yourself at home. Write the number.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up in a lift with a bathroom scale on the floor, the girl holding the rail.
setup.caption: 2. Stand on the scale in the lift. Hold the rail.

setup.art: A close picture of a dial scale with the needle a little past its normal reading, and an arrow showing the lift starting upwards.
setup.caption: 3. Watch the needle as the lift starts to go up.

flow.do: Weigh your child at home on the scale. Write down the number. Ask for a guess about the number in the lift, and a reason.
flow.say: This is your weight on the scale at home. We will stand on it in the lift. Will the number change when the lift starts? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand on the scale and read it. Will the number change in the lift? Why?

ask.q: Do you think the number will change when the lift starts to move? Why?
good: Yes, I think I will feel heavier.
No, I weigh the same everywhere.
I will feel lighter going down.

flow.parent: Many people say the number will not change. Do not correct it. Some digital scales are slow to show a change. A dial scale, or filming the scale, makes it easier to see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lift Scale. You read your weight at home and guess before the ride.

flow.do: In the lift, place the scale on the floor and stand on it. Hold the rail. A grown-up presses a button to go up. Watch the number as the lift starts, as it moves, and as it stops. Write the highest and lowest numbers.
flow.say: Stand still and hold the rail. Watch the number. What does it do as we start? What does it do while we move? What does it do as we stop?
flow.kid: Stand on the scale. Hold the rail. Watch the number as the lift starts, moves and stops.
flow.parent: Stand still. Moving about makes the number jump. A phone filming the scale lets you play it back slowly. Digital scales can be slow or blink, so a dial scale or a filmed scale works best. You may only see a change of a fraction of a kilogram to about a kilogram or two, so look at the moments the lift starts and stops.

check.q: The scale showed more than usual just as the lift started going up. What does that tell you?
options: The scale pushed up on you with more than your weight, because you were speeding up
Your mass got bigger for a moment
Gravity got stronger in the lift
check.why: To speed you up, the scale had to push up with more than the Earth pulls down. The scale reading shows how hard it pushes. Your mass and gravity did not change. The net force upwards is what changed your motion.

flow.context: In this step, you ride the lift up and watch how the scale changes.

flow.do: Ride the lift down in the same way. Watch the number as the lift starts down, as it moves and as it stops. Write the highest and lowest numbers.
flow.say: Now we go down. Watch the number as we start, as we move, and as we stop. What do you notice this time?
flow.kid: Ride the lift down. Watch the number. What does it do as the lift starts and stops?
flow.parent: Going down, the number usually dips as the lift starts, stays normal while it moves, and rises a little as it slows to stop. It is the opposite of going up.
flow.context: In this step, you ride the lift down and watch how the scale changes.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: The number changed only when the lift started or stopped. When it moved at a steady speed, it read as usual. Why do you think that was?
flow.kid: The number changed when the lift started or stopped. Why only then?

ask.q: Why did the scale read as usual when the lift moved at a steady speed?
good: Nothing was changing the motion, so the forces were balanced.
The scale pushed up exactly as hard as the Earth pulled down.
The motion was not changing.

flow.parent: No lift? Stand still on the scale at home, then bend your knees quickly: the number dips, then rises above your weight as you stop bending. Film it. With 2 to 4 children: one stands on the scale, one reads, one films, one writes; swap, but only one child rides at a time. After your child has answered: the number changes only while the motion is changing. At a steady speed, the scale pushes up with exactly your weight, so the forces are balanced. This is the second law again. A change in motion needs a net force.
flow.context: In this step, you find out why the number changed only when the lift started or stopped.

projects.title: Brake Zone: how far does a car go before it stops?
projects.context: In this project, you let a toy car roll down a ramp from three heights onto a towel that acts as its brakes. You measure how far it goes before it stops, and find out why speed matters so much on the road.

materials.item: a smooth board about 1 metre long, and a pile of books to lift one end
a small toy car that rolls freely
a bath towel folded flat, about 1.5 metres long, to be the brake strip
tape to hold the towel and to mark the start of the brake strip
a ruler or measuring tape, and a pencil and paper

projects.safety: Make sure the stack of books cannot fall. Keep fingers away from the bottom of the ramp.

schedule.what: Guess. Build the track. Run the car from three heights. Measure the stopping distances. Chart them and talk about the road.

projects.record: Make a table with three rows, one for each ramp height. Write the middle stopping distance of three runs for each. Draw a bar chart of the three distances.

setup.art: A board resting on a pile of books, with its lower end meeting a flat towel taped to the floor, and a toy car at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Lift one end of the board. Tape the towel at the bottom.

setup.art: A toy car rolling off the end of the board onto the towel, with tape marking where the towel begins.
setup.caption: 2. Let the car go. It rolls onto the towel and stops.

setup.art: A ruler measuring the distance from the tape line to the front of the stopped car, with a pencil mark.
setup.caption: 3. Measure from the tape line to the front of the car.

flow.do: Show your child the car, the ramp and the towel. Say that a car let go from four times the height reaches the bottom at about twice the speed. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: A car let go from four times as high reaches the bottom at about twice the speed. How much further will it go on the towel before it stops? Twice as far? Four times? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Twice the speed. Will the car go twice as far on the towel? Four times? Why?

ask.q: If the car goes twice as fast, how much further do you think it will go before it stops? Why?
good: Twice as far, because it is twice as fast.
More than twice as far.
Four times as far.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say twice as far. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of Brake Zone. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Lift one end of the board by 8 centimetres and check with the ruler. 2. Lay the towel flat on the floor at the bottom, and tape its edge so the car does not bump. 3. Tape a line where the towel begins. 4. Mark a start line near the top of the board.
flow.say: We will build a test track. The car rolls down the board, and the towel is its brake. We measure from the tape line to where the car stops.
flow.kid: Lift the board 8 centimetres. Lay the towel at the bottom. Tape a line where the towel begins.
flow.parent: The car must roll smoothly from the board onto the towel. Fold or tape the towel edge so it does not catch. The towel should be long enough for the highest run. If the car stops before reaching the towel at 4 centimetres, use 6, 12 and 24 centimetres instead. If it rolls off the end of the towel, fold the towel in two so it brakes harder; a thick doormat or a folded blanket also works.

check.q: Why do we measure from the tape line and not from the top of the ramp?
options: The brakes start working at the tape line, so that is where stopping starts
The tape line is easier to see
The ramp is not part of the test
check.why: Stopping distance is measured from where the brakes start. On the board, the car is speeding up. On the towel, it is slowing down. We want to know how far the car goes while it is being stopped.

flow.context: In this step, you build the test track and decide where to measure from.

flow.do: Run the car from the start line at 4 centimetres, then 8 centimetres, then 16 centimetres. Let go of the car, never push it. Measure the distance it goes on the towel. Do 3 runs at each height.
flow.say: Let go of the car at the start line. Where does it stop? Measure from the tape line to the front of the car. Do each height three times.
flow.kid: Let the car go. Measure how far it goes on the towel. Do three runs at each height.
flow.parent: Change the height by changing the books. Check each height with the ruler. Use the middle distance of the three runs. Expect the distances to grow roughly as fast as the heights, but not exactly: this is a rough test. With 2 to 4 children: one releases, one marks the stop with a pencil, one measures, one records. Swap after each height. If the car bounces or skids sideways, tape the board edges as guide rails.
flow.context: In this step, you run the car from three heights and measure how far it goes on the towel.

flow.do: Make a table and draw a bar chart of the middle distances. Ask your child to say or write a claim, evidence and reason.
flow.say: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each height. Say what you found and why.

ask.q: How did the stopping distance change when the speed doubled?
good: It went about four times as far.
It grew faster than the speed.
The distance was about 4 times as long when the speed was twice as big.

check.q: The car from 16 centimetres reached about twice the speed of the car from 4 centimetres. About how many times as far did it go on the towel?
options: About 4 times as far
About 2 times as far
About the same distance
check.why: The towel slows the car by about the same amount every second, whatever its speed. A faster car takes longer to stop, and it also travels faster for all that time. Twice the time and twice the speed make four times the distance.

flow.parent: If your results are messy, say so, and talk about why. Doubling the speed should give about four times the distance, give or take a lot. The pattern to look for is that the distance grows about as fast as the height.
flow.context: In this step, you draw a chart of the three distances and say what the chart shows.

flow.do: Ask the question below. Let your child answer first. Then read the note for the parent.
flow.say: A car goes at 20 kilometres an hour and another at 40, with the same brakes. How much more road does the faster car need? What does this tell a driver?
flow.kid: A car goes twice as fast. How much more road does it need to stop? What should a driver do?

ask.q: A car goes twice as fast as another one, with the same brakes. How much more road does it need to stop? What should a driver do near a school?
good: About four times as much road.
Drive slowly near a school, so there is time to stop.
Leave a big gap in front on a highway.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: with a steady braking force, doubling the speed makes the stopping distance about four times as long. That is why speed limits near schools are low. A loaded vehicle also takes longer to stop, because the same brakes slow a bigger mass by less every second.
flow.context: In this step, you use your test to think about road safety.

challenges.title: The Fastest Cargo Cart: carry a bottle across the table in the shortest time
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a cart from home things that carries a bottle of water across a table, pulled by a small hanging bag. The cart with the shortest time wins.
challenges.problem: Build a cart from home things that carries one 500 millilitre bottle of water 60 centimetres across a table, pulled by a bag with 100 millilitres of water hanging over the table edge. Make the trip take the least time you can.
constraints: Build the cart from home things, not from a ready-made toy.
The cart must carry the bottle of water without it falling off.
The thread is tied to the front of the cart, and the bag holds exactly 100 millilitres of water.
The cart must be no longer than 25 centimetres.
Every cart is timed 3 times, and the best of the three counts.
materials: cardboard, a cereal box or an ice-cream tub lid
4 bottle caps, round pencils or straws, and tape
a 500 millilitre bottle of water, a bag with 100 millilitres of water, and the pulling machine from the Hanging Bag Cart test
a phone or watch with a stopwatch, and a helper
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts any thick cardboard or plastic. Mop up spills at once.
general: A flat cardboard base with four bottle caps for wheels, and the bottle tied on top.
A short, light cart with a low platform, so it does not tip.
A cart with wheels that turn easily, on axles made from straws and pencils.
creative: A cart that is nothing but a very light frame, so almost all the mass is the cargo and the cart itself is as light as it can be.
A cart with smooth round pencils as rollers instead of wheels, to reduce the friction.
Two thin runners made from smooth plastic lids instead of wheels. Does it slide better than it rolls?
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your cart. Build it and time it 3 times. Change one thing, such as the weight of the cart or the way the wheels turn, and time it again. Which change helped most? Why do you think it did?

setup.art: A child sketching three cart designs on paper: a box with bottle-cap wheels, a flat tray on pencils, and a thin frame.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some cart designs on paper.

setup.art: A cardboard cart with four bottle-cap wheels carrying a 500 millilitre bottle, tied to a thread that runs over a table edge to a hanging bag.
setup.caption: 2. Build your cart and fix it to the thread.

setup.art: A helper with a stopwatch beside a table where the cart is racing to a book at the other end.
setup.caption: 3. Time the cart for 60 centimetres. Try again with one change.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three cart designs.
flow.say: You have the same pull every time. How could you make the cart cross the table faster? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: The pull is always the same. Draw some ways to make the cart faster.

ask.q: What would make a cart cross the table in a shorter time?
good: A lighter cart, so there is less mass to speed up.
Wheels that turn more easily, so there is less friction.
A smooth path with nothing to catch.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fastest Cargo Cart challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Tie the thread to the front. Put the 500 millilitre bottle on top. Make sure the wheels turn freely.
flow.say: Build your first cart. The bottle is the cargo, so it must stay on. Check that the wheels turn easily before you test it.
flow.kid: Build your cart. Tie on the bottle. Spin the wheels. Do they turn easily?
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the cardboard. Wheels that rub on the base waste the pull. Tape the axle loosely so the wheels spin. Keep the cart under 25 centimetres.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design.

flow.do: Time the cart 3 times and write down the best time. Change one thing, such as the weight or the wheels. Time it 3 times again.
flow.say: Time your cart three times. Write down your best time. That is the time to beat. Now change one thing and try again.
flow.kid: Time your cart three times. Write the best time. Change one thing. Time it again.
flow.parent: Change only one thing at a time, or you will not know which change helped. Many carts do better after the cart itself is made lighter, since only the bottle needs to be carried.

check.q: Your cart got faster after you cut a lot of cardboard off it. What is the best reason?
options: The same pull now had less mass to speed up
The bag got heavier
The bottle got lighter
check.why: The bag, the bottle and the thread stayed the same. The cart had less mass, so the same pull changed the speed by more every second.

flow.context: In this step, you test your cart and improve it with one change at a time.

flow.do: Compare carts. Ask which change helped most. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which change helped most? What does this tell you about force and mass?
flow.kid: Which change helped most? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which change helped most, and what does that tell you about force and mass?
good: Making the cart lighter helped, because the same pull changes a smaller mass more.
Better wheels helped, because less of the pull was lost to friction.
Both mattered.

flow.context: In this step, you compare designs and say what they tell you about force and mass.

items.p: Kavya pulls two carts with the same bag of water. One cart is empty and one carries a full bottle. Which statement is right?
opts: The empty cart speeds up more every second
The loaded cart speeds up more every second
Both speed up the same, because the pull is the same
items.why: The same pull changes a bigger mass by less. The loaded cart has more mass, so it speeds up less. Picking 'the same' forgets that mass matters as well as the pull.

items.p: The unit that scientists use for force is the ____.
items.why: The newton is named after Isaac Newton. A small apple weighs about 1 newton.

items.p: Ananya says, 'A bigger force makes a thing travel at a bigger steady speed.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A steady force keeps changing the speed, so the thing goes faster and faster. A steady speed on a rough floor happens when the push matches friction. A force changes the speed. It does not set the speed.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Force
a push or a pull
Mass
how much matter a thing has
Acceleration
how quickly speed or direction changes
Net force
all the forces on a thing added together
Balanced forces
forces that cancel, so the motion does not change
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each, such as the bag's pull for force and the loaded cart for mass.

items.p: Anjali lists six moments. Sort each one: is the net force zero, or not zero?
cats: The net force is not zero
items: A book rests on a table
The net force is not zero
A cyclist rides at a steady speed on a flat road
A bus brakes to stop at a signal
The net force is not zero
A helicopter hovers in one place
The net force is not zero
items.why: Whenever motion changes, the net force is not zero. Whenever a thing stays still or keeps a steady speed in a straight line, the forces cancel. A strong answer says the book has two forces on it, but they are equal.

items.p: A cart has a mass of 4 kilograms. A net force of 12 newtons acts on it. How much does its speed grow every second, in metres per second?
items.why: Acceleration is force divided by mass. 12 divided by 4 is 3. The cart's speed grows by 3 metres per second every second.

items.p: Rani says a stone falls faster than a feather because it is heavier. Where would a stone and a feather fall together?
opts: On the Moon, where there is no air
On a windy day on a hill
Underwater in a bucket
items.why: The feather falls slowly because air pushes up on it. With no air, nothing slows the feather, and both gain speed at the same rate. In 1971, a hammer and a feather landed together on the Moon.

items.p: Put the steps of the Hanging Bag Cart test in order.
items: Time the cart three times with each bag
Guess what a bigger bag and a bigger load will do
Build the machine with the pen, the thread and the bag
Change only the load, and time it again
Say what you found and why
a: Guess what a bigger bag and a bigger load will do
Build the machine with the pen, the thread and the bag
Time the cart three times with each bag
Change only the load, and time it again
Say what you found and why
items.why: First guess, so the test can surprise you. Then build the machine, change one thing at a time, and last say what you found and why.

items.p: In the Hanging Bag Cart test, you put more water in the bag. Say what happened to the cart's time, and why. Use the words 'net force'.
items.a: The time got shorter. More water in the bag means a bigger pull, so the net force on the cart is bigger. A bigger net force changes the cart's speed by more every second, so the cart crosses the table sooner.
items.why: A strong answer says that the time got shorter, links the bigger bag to a bigger net force, and says that the net force changes the speed by more every second.

items.p: Three of these have a net force of zero. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A book on a table
A cycle at a steady speed on a flat road
A helicopter hovering
A rocket just after lift-off
items.why: The rocket's engines push up harder than the Earth pulls down, so the net force is upwards and the rocket speeds up. In the other three, the forces cancel.

items.p: Here is a picture of the Hanging Bag Cart machine. Label each part with its job.
a: the bag of water: gives the pull
the bottles on the cart: the load, which adds mass
the thread over the pen: passes the pull to the cart
the book at the end: the stopper that marks the finish
items.why: The bag's weight is the pull. The bottles add mass, not pull. The thread passes the pull to the cart. The book marks the end of the trip. A strong answer says why the bottles are called a load.
items.art: A table with a ball-pen taped across its edge, a thread over it from a cart with two bottles to a hanging bag, and a book at the far end, each part with an empty label box.

items.p: A cart is pulled forward along a table by a thread with 5 newtons. Friction pulls back with 2 newtons. Show the two forces along the table.
items.obj: a cart pulled along a table by a thread
options: pull of the thread
friction
magnetism
a push from the wall
items.why: The thread pulls forward with 5 newtons and friction pulls back with 2. The net force is 3 newtons forward, so the cart speeds up. If the two forces were equal, the cart would keep a steady speed.

items.p: Anitha lands from a small jump with straight legs, and it hurts her knees. Why does bending the knees help?
opts: The stop takes longer, so the force on the body is smaller
Bending makes the body lighter
Bent knees stop the Earth pulling
items.why: The body goes from its speed to zero either way. Bending the knees makes the stop take more time. A change in motion spread over more time needs a smaller force. The body does not get lighter.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi talk about a loaded cart and an empty cart rolling down the same smooth ramp.

views.says: The loaded cart will be slower. It is heavier, so it is harder to get moving.
They will arrive together. The ramp pulls the heavier cart harder, so it makes up for the extra mass.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you saw on the ramp. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Farhan, using evidence: in the ramp test the loaded cart took about the same time as the empty cart. It is fair to Lakshmi: on a table, pulled by the same bag, the heavier cart is slower, so heavy things are harder to get moving. On the ramp, the pull itself grows with the weight.
items.why: Both friends have noticed something real. Only a test that changes the load on a ramp can tell the difference between the pull staying the same and the pull growing with the mass.

items.p: On a space station, an astronaut pushes a large floating box. What happens?
opts: The box is hard to get moving, because it has a lot of mass
The box moves easily, because it has no weight and so no mass
The box does not move at all in space
items.why: Weightless things still have mass. A large box on the space station is hard to get moving and hard to stop. Weight is the pull of gravity. Mass is how much matter a thing has, and it resists a change in motion everywhere.

items.p: Draw two carts pulled by the same bag of water, one empty and one loaded with a bottle. Draw a longer arrow beside the cart that speeds up more every second.
items.a: Two carts side by side, each with a thread to a bag. The empty cart has the longer arrow.
items.why: The same pull changes the empty cart's motion by more, so it speeds up more every second. A strong drawing shows the same thread and bag on both carts, and the longer arrow on the empty cart.
items.art: Two empty cart outlines side by side with a bag hanging from each, and space for the child to add a bottle and an arrow.

items.p: A 2 kilogram cart gains 3 metres per second every second. What is the net force on it, in newtons?
items.why: Force is mass times acceleration. 2 times 3 is 6. The net force is 6 newtons.

items.p: A net force of 10 newtons acts on a cart with a mass of 5 kilograms. By how much does its speed grow every second, in metres per second?
items.why: Acceleration is force divided by mass. 10 divided by 5 is 2. The speed grows by 2 metres per second every second.

items.p: The same net force acts on a 1 kilogram cart and a 4 kilogram cart. The 1 kilogram cart gains 8 metres per second every second. How much does the 4 kilogram cart gain every second?
opts: 2 metres per second
4 metres per second
32 metres per second
items.why: The 4 kilogram cart has 4 times the mass, so it gains one quarter as much. 8 divided by 4 is 2. Picking 32 multiplies instead of dividing.

items.p: A cart is pulled with 6 newtons against friction of 2 newtons. What is the net force?
opts: 8 newtons
4 newtons
2 newtons
items.why: The pull is forward and the friction is backward, so friction takes away from the pull. 6 take away 2 is 4. Adding them is the most common slip.

items.p: Heena says, 'A bottle has less mass on the Moon because it weighs less there.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The bottle weighs about 6 times less on the Moon, because the Moon pulls less. Its mass, the amount of matter in it, does not change. It would be just as hard to push on the Moon as on Earth.

items.p: Suppose a car needs 5 metres to stop from 20 kilometres an hour, with a steady braking force. About how many metres would it need from 40 kilometres an hour?
opts: 10 metres
20 metres
40 metres
items.why: Twice the speed needs about 4 times the stopping distance. 5 times 4 is 20 metres. Picking 10 metres doubles the distance when the speed doubles, which forgets that a faster car also takes longer to stop.

items.p: Sort each change: does it make the change in speed each second bigger or smaller?
items: Double the pull on the same cart
Double the load on the cart, with the same pull
A rocket burns fuel while its engines push as before
A rickshaw takes on two passengers, with the same pull
A rough doormat is taken away from under a pulled cart
A second rider climbs on a cycle with the same brakes
items.why: A bigger net force makes the change bigger, and a bigger mass makes it smaller. Taking away the doormat leaves more of the pull as net force. Burning fuel leaves less mass for the same push. A second rider adds mass to the braking cycle.

items.p: A rocket gets lighter as it burns fuel, so the same push gives it more ____.
items.why: The push stays about the same while the mass falls. A smaller mass changes its speed by more every second, which is more acceleration.

items.p: An astronaut gives the same push to a floating box of tools and to a floating empty box. What happens?
opts: The box of tools changes its speed less
Both change their speed by the same amount
The box of tools floats away faster
items.why: The box of tools has more mass. The same push changes a bigger mass by less. Both boxes are weightless, so weight does not matter. Mass does.

items.p: A girl says, 'If a cart rolls at a steady speed, no forces are acting on it.' Is she right? Explain using the words 'balanced' and 'friction'.
items.a: She is not right. A cart rolling at a steady speed on a table still has forces on it. If the pull of the thread and the friction are equal, they are balanced, so the net force is zero and the speed does not change. If there were no friction, no pull would be needed.
items.why: A strong answer says that forces are acting, but they are balanced. 'No change' in motion means a net force of zero, not zero forces.

items.p: Draw a cyclist riding at a steady speed along a flat road. Draw the forces along the road as arrows. Make the arrows the right lengths.
items.a: A cyclist with an arrow pointing forward and an arrow of the same length pointing back.
items.why: At a steady speed the net force is zero. The push forward from the legs and the road equals the push back from the air and friction, so the two arrows are the same length.
items.art: A side view of a girl on a cycle on a flat road, with empty space in front and behind for arrows.

items.p: Two friends in Madurai talk about what a force is.

views.says: A force is a real thing. You can feel it when you push a wall.
Nobody has ever seen a force. We only see things move, or springs stretch. A force is a name for the reason a motion changes.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about the cart and the bag. Then say what the other friend has right.
items.a: Either answer is fine if it is backed by evidence. A strong answer agrees with Meenakshi by saying that we feel pushes and pulls with our bodies, and the cart speeds up when the bag pulls. It credits Aarti by saying that what we measure is the cart's change in motion, or a spring's stretch, and a force is how we explain them.
items.why: Scientists still discuss this. Ernst Mach pointed out in 1883 that the second law can be read as a way of defining force. Both friends have noticed something true.

items.p: Match each safety idea to the reason it works.
pairs: Foam inside a cycle helmet
it squashes slowly, so the head takes longer to stop
A seatbelt
it holds you to the seat, so you stop with the car
A crumple zone at the front of a car
it squashes, so the car takes longer to stop
A low speed limit near a school
a slower car needs much less road to stop
A big gap behind a lorry on a highway
a heavy fast vehicle needs a long road to stop
items.why: All five ideas come from the second law. A longer stop needs a smaller force, a lower speed needs a much shorter stop, and a bigger mass needs more road.

items.p: In the made-up example, the 100 millilitre bag took 1.8 seconds and the 400 millilitre bag took 0.8 seconds. How many seconds shorter was the trip with the bigger bag?
items.why: 1.8 take away 0.8 is 1.0. The trip took 1 second less.

items.p: Four times the pull should take about half the time. If a trip takes 1.8 seconds with the 100 millilitre bag, about how long would you expect with the 400 millilitre bag, if friction did not matter?
opts: 0.45 seconds
0.9 seconds
1.4 seconds
items.why: Four times the acceleration makes the trip take half the time, because the time depends on the square root of the acceleration. Half of 1.8 is 0.9. In a real test, friction changes the numbers a little.

items.p: Here is a picture of a cart on a table that is being pulled by a thread. Label the four forces on the cart.
a: push of the table: upward, equal to the weight
items.why: The weight and the table's push are equal, so they cancel. The pull and friction act along the table. When the pull is bigger than friction, the net force is forward, and the cart speeds up.
items.art: A toy cart on a table with a thread pulling it to the right, with four empty label boxes and four short lines pointing to the cart.

items.p: Three of these are changes in motion. Which one is not?
opts: A bus slows down for a stop
A bus turns a corner at a steady speed
A bus travels along a straight road at a steady speed
A bus starts from a stop
items.why: A change in motion means a change in speed or direction. Slowing down, turning and starting are all changes. A steady speed in a straight line is not.

items.p: A bag of 200 millilitres of water pulls a cart across a table in 1.2 seconds. Which change would make the trip take the least time?
opts: Take one bottle off the cart
Use a longer thread
Paint the cart a bright colour
items.why: Taking a bottle off lowers the mass, so the same pull changes the speed by more every second. A longer thread does nothing to the pull or the mass, and paint does not matter.

items.p: A cart has a mass of 1 kilogram. The thread pulls it forward with 7 newtons and friction pulls back with 2 newtons. By how much does its speed grow every second, in metres per second?
items.why: The net force is 7 take away 2, which is 5 newtons. 5 divided by 1 kilogram is 5. The speed grows by 5 metres per second every second.

items.p: A cart has a mass of 2 kilograms. A thread pulls it with 8 newtons and friction pulls back with 2 newtons. By how much does its speed grow every second, in metres per second?
items.why: The net force is 8 take away 2, which is 6 newtons. 6 divided by 2 kilograms is 3. The speed grows by 3 metres per second every second.

items.p: A bathroom scale in a lift reads more than usual just after the lift starts going up. Why?
opts: The lift is speeding up, so the scale has to push up on you with more than your weight
Your mass increases when you go up
Gravity gets stronger in a lift
items.why: To speed you up, the scale must push up with more than the Earth pulls down. The scale shows how hard it pushes. Your mass and the Earth's pull do not change.

items.p: In a lift moving up at a steady speed, a bathroom scale reads more than it does when the lift is at rest. True or false?
items.why: False. At a steady speed, the forces on you are balanced, so the scale pushes up with exactly your weight. It reads more only while the lift is speeding up.

items.p: On the table, the loaded cart was slower. On the ramp, the loaded cart was not slower. Explain the difference using the words 'the pull' and 'the mass'.
items.a: On the table, the pull came from a bag of water that did not change, so a loaded cart had more mass and the same pull, and it sped up less. On the ramp, the pull is part of the cart's own weight, so a loaded cart is pulled harder. The bigger pull and the bigger mass cancel, so both carts speed up equally.
items.why: A strong answer says that on the table the pull stayed the same while the mass grew, and that on the ramp the pull grew with the mass.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad talk about the hammer and feather dropped on the Moon in 1971.

views.says: They landed together because there is no gravity on the Moon.
There is gravity on the Moon. They landed together because there is no air to slow the feather.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about weight, mass and air. Then say what the other friend has noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Kabir. The Moon has gravity, about one sixth of the Earth's, which is why things fall there. They fell together because nothing pushed up on the feather. It credits Anika for noticing that the Moon is different from the Earth, and that without air things fall differently from what we see at home.
items.why: Anika has mixed up gravity and air. The Moon pulls things down, and the astronauts' hammer fell. Only the lack of air let the feather keep up.

items.p: Suppose a car needs 4 metres to stop from 20 kilometres an hour, with a steady braking force. About how far would it need from 60 kilometres an hour?
opts: 12 metres
36 metres
24 metres
items.why: Three times the speed needs 3 times 3, which is 9 times the stopping distance. 4 times 9 is 36 metres. Picking 12 metres only multiplies by 3.

items.p: The same net force of 12 newtons acts on three carts. Put the carts in order, from the one that gains the least speed every second to the one that gains the most.
items.why: Acceleration is force divided by mass. 12 divided by 6 is 2. 12 divided by 3 is 4. 12 divided by 2 is 6. The lightest cart gains the most.

items.p: A fielder catches a fast ball. Draw two catches side by side, one with hands that do not move back and one with hands that move back. Mark which catch has the longer stop.
items.a: Two pictures of a fielder. In the second, the hands are drawn moving back with an arrow, and the second catch is marked as the longer stop.
items.why: Moving the hands back makes the ball take longer to stop. The same change in motion over more time needs a smaller force, so the catch is gentler.
items.art: Two side-by-side outlines of a cricket fielder with hands out, ready to catch, and space for the child to draw the ball and arrows.

items.p: Sort each safety item: does it make the stop take longer, or does it hold you to the vehicle?
items: Bending your knees when you land
A crumple zone at the front of a car
A strap on a child seat
Pulling your hands back in a catch
items.why: Foam, bent knees, crumple zones and soft hands all spread a stop over more time, so the force is smaller. A seatbelt and a child seat strap keep you with the vehicle, so you stop with it and not by hitting something.

items.p: At the edge of some galaxies, stars move faster than the matter we can see should allow. What is one idea scientists have for this?
opts: There may be unseen dark matter pulling on them
Stars at the edge are heavier
Newton's laws do not exist there
items.why: Most astronomers think unseen dark matter is pulling on the stars. A few physicists think the second law itself may change for extremely faint pulls. Nobody has settled the question.

items.p: A force of 1 ____ gives a mass of 1 kilogram a speed gain of 1 metre per second every second.
items.why: This is how the newton is defined. One newton on a 1 kilogram mass gives it an acceleration of 1 metre per second every second.

items.p: A 1 kilogram bottle of water weighs about how many newtons?
opts: 10 newtons
1 newton
100 newtons
items.why: A small apple of about 100 grams weighs about 1 newton. A bottle of 1 kilogram has 10 times as much mass, so it weighs about 10 newtons.

items.p: When you jump, the floor pushes you up and you push the floor down. Why can nobody see the Earth move?
items.a: The Earth does move, but it has so much mass that the same push changes its motion by an amount far too small to see. A person has very little mass, so the same push changes their motion a lot.
items.why: A strong answer uses the second law. The same size of force changes a very big mass by a tiny amount.

items.p: Here is a picture of a rocket on its way up. Label what each arrow shows.
labels: arrow pointing up from the engine
arrow pointing down from the middle
the part that gets smaller as fuel burns
a: arrow pointing up from the engine: thrust
arrow pointing down from the middle: weight
the fuel tanks: most of the rocket's mass at the start
the part that gets smaller as fuel burns: the mass of the rocket
items.why: The thrust is bigger than the weight, so the net force is upwards. As the fuel burns, the mass shrinks, and the same thrust speeds the rocket up more.

quiz.p: A cart is pulled with a net force. The net force is doubled and the cart is the same. What happens to the change in speed each second?
opts: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
quiz.why: Twice the net force gives twice the acceleration. Picking 'halves' mixes up force and mass.

quiz.p: The same pull acts on a cart. A load is added so the cart's mass is three times as big. What happens to the change in speed each second?
opts: It becomes one third
It triples
It stays the same
quiz.why: Three times the mass gives one third of the acceleration for the same net force. Picking 'triples' reverses the rule.

quiz.p: In the Hanging Bag Cart test, which change makes the cart's trip take less time?
opts: More water in the bag
More bottles on the cart
Starting the cart further back
quiz.why: More water is a bigger pull, so the cart's speed changes by more every second. More bottles slow it down, and starting further back makes the trip longer.

quiz.p: Which of these is a change in motion?
opts: A bus going round a bend at a steady speed
A bus parked at a stand
A bus going straight at a steady speed
quiz.why: A change in motion is a change in speed or in direction. Going round a bend changes the direction every moment, even if the speed stays the same.

quiz.p: A heavy ball and a light ball are dropped together in a place with no air. What happens?
opts: They land together
The heavy one lands first
The light one lands first
quiz.why: The Earth pulls the heavy ball harder, but it also has more mass, so the two cancel. Both gain speed at the same rate.

quiz.p: A cyclist rides at a steady speed on a flat road. What is true of the forces along the road?
opts: The forward push equals the backward push
There is only a forward push
There are no forces at all
quiz.why: At a steady speed the net force is zero. The forces are balanced, not missing.

quiz.p: Two cycles have the same brakes, squeezing with the same force. The cycle with two riders needs a longer road to stop than the cycle with one rider. True or false?
quiz.why: True. The same braking force slows a bigger mass by less every second, so the cycle with two riders takes more road to stop.

quiz.p: A rocket's engines push with the same force while it burns fuel. What happens to its acceleration?
opts: It gets bigger, because the mass gets smaller
It gets smaller, because the fuel is gone
It stays the same
quiz.why: The same push acts on a smaller mass, so the speed changes by more every second.

quiz.p: A net force of 15 newtons acts on a cart with a mass of 3 kilograms. By how much does its speed grow every second, in metres per second?
quiz.why: Acceleration is force divided by mass. 15 divided by 3 is 5. The speed grows by 5 metres per second every second.

quiz.p: Which question about the second law do scientists still argue about?
opts: Does the law change for very faint pulls far out in galaxies?
Does a bigger force change motion more?
Do heavy things fall faster than light things?
quiz.why: The first two are settled by countless tests. Whether the law changes for extremely faint pulls is an open question, linked to the puzzle of dark matter.

quiz.p: A bag of water pulls three carts. Put the carts in order, from the one that speeds up most to the one that speeds up least.
quiz.why: The pull is the same, so the cart with the least mass speeds up most. More bottles mean more mass, so the cart speeds up less.

quiz.p: A book rests on a table. Which statement is right?
opts: The Earth pulls it down and the table pushes it up equally
Only the Earth pulls on it
The table pushes up harder than the Earth pulls down
quiz.why: The book is not moving, so the net force is zero. The table's push upwards must equal the Earth's pull downwards.

quiz.p: On a smooth ramp, a cart with three bottles and an empty cart are let go together. What happens?
opts: They take about the same time
The loaded cart takes much longer
The empty cart takes much longer
quiz.why: The ramp pulls the loaded cart harder, and the loaded cart also has more mass. The two cancel, so both carts speed up at about the same rate.

applications: Engineers use force equals mass times acceleration to choose the engines for cars, trains, ships and rockets.
Lorry and bus drivers keep a big gap on highways, because heavy fast vehicles need a long road to stop.
Speed limits near schools are low, because a car at half the speed needs about a quarter of the road to stop.
Heavy goods trains on the railways are pulled by more than one engine, so that the pull is big enough for the mass.
Lift makers start and stop lifts gently, because a sudden start would push up on your feet far harder than your own weight.
Seatbelts, airbags, crumple zones and helmet foam make a stop take longer, so the force on the body is smaller.
Cricket fielders pull their hands back when they catch, and high jumpers land on thick mats.
ISRO plans the path of its rockets and of Mangalyaan with Newton's laws of motion.
Cranes, ropes and chains are chosen to be strong enough for the weight of the load plus the extra pull needed to start it moving.
Packers load heavy things low and tied down, because a heavy load that starts or stops suddenly needs a big force to hold it.

open_questions.q: Why do things have mass, and why does mass resist a change in motion?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure mass extremely well, and they know that much of the mass of ordinary things comes from the energy inside atoms. But a full answer to why mass resists changes in motion is still being worked on.

open_questions.q: Why does the mass that resists a push match the mass that the Earth pulls on, so exactly?
open_questions.why_open: Tests have shown the two masses to be equal to an extremely tiny fraction. Einstein's general theory of relativity builds on this match, but a deeper reason may need a theory that joins gravity with quantum physics, and nobody has one yet.

open_questions.q: Does the second law change for extremely faint pulls, such as those at the edge of a galaxy?
open_questions.why_open: Most astronomers think unseen dark matter explains why stars at the edge of galaxies move so fast. A minority think the law itself changes there. Neither idea has been proved, and new observations keep testing both.

open_questions.q: Is a force a real thing in the world, or only a useful name for why a motion changes?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists and philosophers still disagree. Some say the forces are real, and some say the laws of motion define the word force. The cart tests cannot settle this, because they only show changes in motion.

open_questions.q: Are the laws of motion the same everywhere in the universe, and were they the same long ago?
open_questions.why_open: Observations of far-away galaxies and of light that left them billions of years ago show no change so far. Scientists keep checking, because even a tiny difference would be a major discovery.

open_questions.q: Do all the forces we know, such as pushes, pulls, friction and gravity, come from a smaller set of basic forces?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have joined several forces into one, such as electricity and magnetism. Whether gravity can join them is still an open question.

maths.problem: In the made-up example, the middle times for the 100, 200 and 400 millilitre bags were 1.8, 1.2 and 0.8 seconds. How many seconds shorter was the trip with the 200 millilitre bag than with the 100 millilitre bag? How many seconds shorter with the 400 millilitre bag than with the 200 millilitre bag? Which step saved more time?
maths.answer: 0.6 seconds, then 0.4 seconds. The first step saved more time.
maths.explain: 1.8 take away 1.2 is 0.6. 1.2 take away 0.8 is 0.4. The second step added more water, 200 millilitres against 100, but it saved less time. The more pull you already have, the less each extra bit of pull saves.
maths.context: This is about the Hanging Bag Cart test. A bag of water pulls a cart across a table, and you time the trip with three different bags.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the steps between your times shows a pattern that the times alone do not: extra pull helps less and less.

maths.problem: A cart with a mass of 1 kilogram gains 3 metres per second every second when the net force is 3 newtons. How much does it gain with 6 newtons, 9 newtons and 12 newtons? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 6, 9 and 12 metres per second every second. For this cart, the gain in metres per second every second is the same number as the force in newtons.
maths.explain: Doubling the force from 3 to 6 doubled the gain from 3 to 6. Tripling it to 9 tripled the gain. For a 1 kilogram cart, force in newtons and acceleration are the same number. The gain goes up in step with the force.
maths.context: This is about the second law. A bigger pull on the same cart makes its speed change more every second.
maths.why_maths: A times table shows how the second law scales: twice the force gives twice the gain, three times the force gives three times the gain.

maths.problem: A net force of 24 newtons acts on four different carts with masses of 2, 3, 4 and 6 kilograms. How much does each cart gain in speed every second? What happens to the gain when the mass doubles from 3 to 6 kilograms?
maths.answer: 12, 8, 6 and 4 metres per second every second. When the mass doubles from 3 to 6 kilograms, the gain halves, from 8 to 4.
maths.explain: Divide 24 by each mass. 24 divided by 2 is 12. 24 divided by 3 is 8. 24 divided by 4 is 6. 24 divided by 6 is 4. A bigger mass gives a smaller gain, and twice the mass gives half the gain.
maths.context: This is about the load part of the Hanging Bag Cart test. The same pull acts on carts with different loads.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the same force by different masses shows the rule 'twice the mass, half the change' with real numbers.

maths.problem: Suppose a car needs 3 metres to stop from 10 kilometres an hour. Each time the speed doubles, the stopping distance is multiplied by 4. Write the stopping distances for 10, 20, 40 and 80 kilometres an hour.
maths.answer: 3, 12, 48 and 192 metres. These are made-up numbers, to show the pattern.
maths.explain: 3 times 4 is 12. 12 times 4 is 48. 48 times 4 is 192. The speed only doubles each time, but the distance is multiplied by 4. A small rise in speed makes a big difference to the road a driver needs.
maths.context: This is about the Brake Zone project. You let a car roll onto a towel from three heights, and the faster car goes much further before it stops.
maths.why_maths: A growing pattern lets you predict a stopping distance for a speed you have not tested, which is what a road engineer needs.

maths.problem: In the Hanging Bag Cart test, you time 5 different settings, 3 times each. How many timings is that? If each timing takes 90 seconds, including putting the cart back, how many minutes does it take in all?
maths.answer: 15 timings, and 22 and a half minutes.
maths.explain: 5 times 3 is 15 timings. 15 times 90 seconds is 1,350 seconds. 1,350 divided by 60 is 22 with 30 left over, so 22 and a half minutes. This is why the test takes most of 40 minutes.
maths.context: This is about planning the Hanging Bag Cart test, where every setting is timed three times.
maths.why_maths: Counting the timings and their total time shows how long a fair test really takes, so you can plan the session.

maths.problem: About 100 millilitres of water pulls with a force of about 1 newton. About how many newtons do the 200 millilitre and the 400 millilitre bags pull with? What about a bag with 250 millilitres?
maths.explain: 100 millilitres gives about 1 newton. 200 millilitres is 2 times as much, so about 2 newtons. 400 millilitres is 4 times as much, so about 4 newtons. 250 millilitres is 2.5 times as much, so about 2.5 newtons.
maths.context: This is about the bags in the Hanging Bag Cart test, which hang from the thread and pull the cart.
maths.why_maths: A ratio turns the water in a bag into the force of its pull, so you can say how many times bigger one pull is than another.

maths.problem: Each bottle on the cart has a mass of about 500 grams. What is the total mass of three bottles in kilograms? About how many newtons does the Earth pull them with, if 100 grams is pulled with about 1 newton?
maths.explain: 3 times 500 grams is 1,500 grams, which is 1.5 kilograms. 1,500 divided by 100 is 15. So the Earth pulls the three bottles with about 15 newtons.
maths.context: This is about the load in the Hanging Bag Cart test. The bottles on the cart add mass.
maths.why_maths: Changing grams to kilograms and then to newtons lets you compare the load with the pull of the bag.

maths.problem: Draw a bar chart of the made-up middle times 1.8, 1.2 and 0.8 seconds. Use 1 centimetre for every 0.2 seconds. How tall is each bar?
maths.explain: 1.8 divided by 0.2 is 9. 1.2 divided by 0.2 is 6. 0.8 divided by 0.2 is 4. The shortest bar is the quickest trip, from the biggest bag.
maths.context: This is about the results chart of the Hanging Bag Cart test, with one bar for each bag.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which bag gave the quickest trip, and by how much.

maths.problem: A cart is pulled with a net force. The net force is doubled, and the cart gets three bottles of extra load, which makes its mass 3 times as big. Is the change in speed each second bigger or smaller than before? By what fraction?
maths.answer: Smaller. It is 2 out of 3 as big, or two thirds of what it was.
maths.explain: Double the force would double the change. Three times the mass would make it one third as big. 2 times one third is two thirds. So the change in speed each second is two thirds of what it was.
maths.context: This is about the second law. A bigger pull and a bigger load both change how fast the cart speeds up.
maths.why_maths: Fractions let you combine two changes, a bigger force and a bigger mass, into one answer.

how_we_found_out.context: How hard does a moving thing hit, and how far will it go before it stops? This card tells how people found out, and who was left out of the story.
how_we_found_out.story: Around 1700, thinkers argued about how to measure the 'force' of a moving thing. Descartes had taught that it grows in step with the speed: twice the speed, twice the force. Others, following Gottfried Leibniz, said it grows faster. In the 1720s, a Dutch scientist named Willem 's Gravesande dropped brass balls into soft clay. A ball that hit the clay at twice the speed made a dent about four times as deep, he reported. Emilie du Chatelet, a French mathematician and scientist, studied his results. In her book of 1740, she argued that the clay showed that Descartes was wrong, and that a faster ball needs much more than twice the stopping. This is why a car at twice the speed needs about four times the road to stop. In her last years she translated Newton's Principia into French, with her own notes. She finished it in 1749. It was printed after her death, in part in 1756 and in full in 1759.
how_we_found_out.who: Emilie du Chatelet, a French mathematician and scientist (1706 to 1749), and Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch scientist
how_we_found_out.when: The clay experiments in the 1720s, her book in 1740, and her translation of Newton in 1749
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Descartes and his followers taught that the force of a moving thing grows only in step with its speed. The clay showed that a ball at twice the speed makes a dent about four times as deep, so the stopping needed grows much faster than the speed.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Hanging Bag Cart needs a strong wheeled toy that can carry about 1.5 kilograms, three 500 millilitre bottles, a pen taped to the table edge, and a stopwatch. The numbers were worked out from the physics for a toy truck on a smooth table, with a run of 60 centimetres: about 1.5 to 2 seconds with a 100 millilitre bag and two bottles, about 1 second with 200 millilitres, and a little under 1 second with 400 millilitres. Part B should give about 1.2 to 2 seconds as one to three bottles are added. Hand timing is rough, which is why every setting is timed three times and the middle time is used. A flimsy cart, a table edge that catches the thread, or wheels that stick can change the numbers a lot, and the steps say what to do then. The Ramp Surprise should show a clear drop in time as the ramp gets steeper, and almost no change when a load is added. The Brake Zone works best with a small car that rolls freely and a towel. The Lift Scale needs a lift and a grown-up and shows only a small change on a child's scale. Soft Hands uses a soft ball and one low step only. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 90 minutes. Facts to verify before release: the Moon's pull being about one sixth of the Earth's; the date, astronaut and falcon feather of the Apollo 15 hammer and feather drop (August 1971, David Scott); the dent depths reported by 's Gravesande; the dates of Emilie du Chatelet's book and translation; the Mach 1883 and Milgrom 1983 dates.
